papers.title: Mitophagy coordinates organelle crosstalk in health and diseases.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitophagy, the selective removal of damaged mitochondria, interacts with other cellular organelles like the ER, lysosomes, and peroxisomes. It likely discusses signaling pathways that coordinate this organelle crosstalk to maintain cellular health. The review probably also covers how disruptions in these interactions contribute to disease states, including neurodegeneration.
papers.why: Understanding how mitophagy coordinates organelle crosstalk provides mechanistic insight relevant to neuronal mitophagy dysfunction, which could inform interpretation of spatial transcriptomic and metabolomic signatures in interneurons and perineuronal net-associated pathology.

papers.title: SLMO2 promotes chemoresistance in glioblastoma by regulating BNIP3-dependent mitophagy via the NF-κB/HIF-1α axis.
papers.summary: This paper studies SLMO2, a mitochondrial protein, and shows it helps glioblastoma cells resist chemotherapy. It does this by promoting BNIP3-driven mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria, through activation of the NF-κB/HIF-1α signaling pathway. The findings suggest SLMO2 could be a target to overcome drug resistance in brain tumors.
papers.why: This work offers mechanistic insight into BNIP3-dependent mitophagy regulation that may be transferable to understanding mitophagy pathways in neurons, even though the model system is glioblastoma rather than neuronal cells.

papers.title: Innate immune signaling relays environmental cues to mitophagy for metabolic adaptation to obesity.
papers.summary: This paper likely explores how innate immune signaling pathways communicate environmental or dietary signals to mitophagy, the process that clears damaged mitochondria, as a way to help the body metabolically adapt to obesity. It probably identifies specific immune molecules or receptors that act as messengers linking inflammatory cues to mitochondrial quality control in metabolic tissues. The work suggests that mitophagy isn't just a cellular housekeeping process but is actively tuned by immune signals in response to nutrient excess or obesity-related stress.
papers.why: Although focused on obesity and peripheral metabolism rather than neurons, this paper could offer mechanistic insight into immune-mitophagy crosstalk that may be relevant to understanding how neuroinflammation or environmental cues regulate mitochondrial quality control in brain cells, including interneurons.

papers.title: Revisiting Inherited Metabolic Diseases (IMDs) Through the Lens of Selective Autophagy
papers.summary: This paper reconsiders Inherited Metabolic Diseases by examining how selective autophagy pathways, including mitophagy, may be disrupted or altered in these conditions. It likely proposes that defects in selective degradation of damaged organelles and protein aggregates contribute to disease pathology beyond the primary enzymatic deficiencies. The review probably highlights potential therapeutic angles targeting autophagy machinery for these genetic metabolic disorders.
papers.why: Since the PhD project centers on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, this review could offer mechanistic insights and disease models relevant to understanding selective autophagy dysregulation in brain cells.

papers.title: Increasing autophagy with fasting and diet: separating fact from fiction.
papers.summary: This paper critically examines the common claim that fasting and specific diets reliably boost autophagy, a cellular cleanup process. It separates well-supported scientific findings from overstated or unproven claims often circulating in popular health discourse. The review likely clarifies what methods actually have evidence for inducing autophagy versus what remains speculative.
papers.why: Understanding which fasting or dietary interventions genuinely induce autophagy is important context for interpreting mitophagy and autophagy regulation in neurons, especially when designing experiments involving metabolic manipulation.

papers.title: Salidroside regulates hippocampal neuronal autophagy in ASD mice via the SIRT2/FoxO1 pathway.
papers.summary: This study looks at salidroside, a natural compound, and its effects on hippocampal neurons in a mouse model of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The researchers found that salidroside influences autophagy (the cell's process of clearing damaged components) through a specific molecular pathway involving SIRT2 and FoxO1 proteins. The abstract suggests this pathway could be a therapeutic target for ASD-related neuronal dysfunction.
papers.why: This paper connects to the profile's focus on mitophagy and autophagy regulation in neurons, offering a potential molecular pathway (SIRT2/FoxO1) relevant to hippocampal neuronal health that could inform mechanistic studies in the broader research context.
